newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK - U.S. crudes adrift after Iraq pull-back.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK - U.S. crudes adrift after Iraq pull-back.

text.p: U.S. crude prices were still at lofty outright levels early Monday despite an easing in the Iraq crisis, but traders expect further pressure on domestic grade margins as buyers hold out for lower prices.

All eyes were on the Middle East last week, as headline after headline braced oil markets for new U.S. airstrikes, following Iraq's shooting missiles at American fighter planes patrolling "no-fly" zones in northern and southern Iraq.

October crude oil futures contracts on the New York Mercantile Exchange reached a high of $25.35 a barrel, before falling back Friday to close at $24.51 a barrel after Baghdad said it would not fire on U.S. planes patrolling the no-fly zones.
Technical factors, pointing to a vastly overbought market, and profit-taking aided the futures retrench of October NYMEX crude, traders said.

For this week, market players look for an extension of the selling, barring any further Middle East tensions. Traders said as much as $2-$3 a barrel could be lopped off the outright price in the near-term.

Adam Siemenski, vice president at County Nat West Securities in Baltimore, said high demand and low crude and products inventories underpin the market, but the situation went out of control last week.
"(WTI at) $20.00 is the level which balances off most of the political and economic issues involved in establishing oil prices, $15.00 is too low and $25.00 is too high," Siemenski said.
Domestic grades are also expected to weaken, or at least maintain the softer tone established Friday.
Sweet grades featured a widespread weakening for Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire, which was done at parity to WTI/Cushing Friday, some 20-25 cts weaker than previous deals.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James fell back below a 30 cts premium to the WTI, while Midland/WTI was talked at only pennies over the benchmark.
Sour grades also shaved around 5 cts off their differentials to the WTI/Cushing.
"The margins are sickly. The grades will be biting heavily (this week)," said a Houston oil broker.

Arbitrage opportunities for bringing over Brent barrels from Europe have been mixed. Even as the spread between October and November Brent and WTI narrowed to around $1.00, the dated price fell to deals at 35 cts under.

There was, however, rampant talk that a million-barrel Brent load was being shipped to the U.S. Gulf late last week, though the rumored Wall Street trader thought in possession of the Brent cargo wouldn't confirm.
Traders were reminded that the suspension of the U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food accord is an ancillary bullish factor resulting from revitalized Iraqi military moves.

Many crude traders had been expecting limited Iraqi exports in the market by mid-September, but the unsafe conditions on the ground in Iraq resulted in the United Nations indefinitely suspending the deal on Sept. 1.
When, and if, the oil for aid plan is implemented, some 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude will appear on the market.

Under the oil-for-food accord, Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude over a renewable six-month period, in order to purchase supplies for civilians suffering from crippling sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
